progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b06c and B6b: a gene is transcribed and translated to make a protein; RNA pairs with DNA by complementary bases (A with U, C with G). From bio-m5 inheritance (B9, B10): a heterozygous parent passes each allele to about half its offspring, because each gamete gets one chromosome of a pair. From b01 and b03 (Module 6): sickle cell is a single-base missense mutation in the beta-globin gene; sickle haemoglobin distorts red cells. From b05: somatic mutations are not inherited; germ-line mutations can be. From b09: gene editing changes a chosen stretch of DNA; biotechnology spans medicine, agriculture and industry. From b10: judging a technology by benefit, harm and who gets each; checking what a technology actually did. Not assumed: guide RNA, Cas9, foetal haemoglobin, BCL11A, ex vivo editing, gene drive, the evidence ladder, need, feasibility and fairness.
progression.startsWith: Move from an existing technique to a proposed future use. The video opens: In late 2023, a treatment made with the gene-editing tool CRISPR was approved for the first time, for sickle cell disease.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining how CRISPR edits DNA (a guide RNA pairs with the target, Cas9 cuts both strands, repair often adds or loses bases) and that it can cut similar stretches elsewhere; explaining the approved sickle cell treatment (stem cells edited outside the body so less BCL11A is made, foetal haemoglobin returns and prevents most sickling, the sickle allele remains) and its evidence; explaining why working in a trial is not the same as being available to everyone (chemotherapy, hospital time, cost, where patients live); sorting claims by how far the evidence has got; explaining that gene editing suits problems caused by one gene, not most common diseases; explaining how a gene drive spreads to nearly all offspring and could crash a mosquito population, its caged evidence and its uncertainties (resistance, ecological effects, borders and consent, reversal); judging a future use by need, feasibility and fairness and phrasing it as "could, if"; applying this to an unseen in-body editing item and an unseen overclaiming headline.
progression.nextLesson: how genetic techniques can change biodiversity at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels (route entry bio-m6-b12).

teaching.task: A CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease is already approved, and headlines promise far more. So which future uses of biotechnology are plausible, and how can you tell?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: how CRISPR finds its target (base pairing of the guide, 2); why repair can switch a stretch off (bases added or lost, 2); why off-target cuts happen (the guide pairs with a similar stretch, 2); why the sickle cell treatment works without fixing the allele (foetal haemoglobin returns when its switch is reduced, 3); why it is not available to everyone (chemotherapy, hospital time, cost, where patients live, 4); why editing suits single-gene conditions (one stretch to change, 5); how a gene drive beats half-and-half inheritance (it copies itself to the other chromosome, 6); how it can crash a population (homozygous females cannot breed, 7); why its success is uncertain (resistance, ecology, consent, reversal, 8). Visible case: one ladder; the two cases sit on different rungs. Video advantage: the guide zipping onto DNA, the drive band copying across, the offspring row filling from half to all, the population line falling. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 1 card is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: A CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease is already approved while headlines promise far more, so the question is which future uses are plausible and how to tell; CRISPR is shown finding its target with a guide RNA and cutting with Cas9, the approved sickle cell treatment shows what an existing use looks like (the foetal haemoglobin switch, edited outside the body) with its evidence and its catch (cost, hospital time, where patients live), the evidence ladder places each direction from idea to approved, a malaria gene drive is the proposed future use (how it beats the half-and-half rule and could crash a population, caged evidence only) with its unknowns, and need, feasibility and fairness give a "could, if" judgement. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In late 2023, a treatment made with the gene-editing tool CRISPR was approved for the first time, for sickle cell disease. Since then, the claims have grown: CRISPR will wipe out malaria, cure every genetic disease, end crop failure. Some of these could happen, and some are hype. So which future uses of biotechnology are plausible, and how can you tell?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is an explain-and-identify item on a gene-editing treatment for high cholesterol delivered to the liver (the gene's effect on cholesterol is given on the card): explain the mechanism of benefit and identify two uncertainties. It tests the route stop on a new case. 11c is an evaluate item on the headline "CRISPR will soon cure all genetic diseases". It tests scene 9's judgement and the "could, if" wording. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ2-01: "investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)", with the two listed sub-points this video carries: "researching future directions of the use of biotechnology" and "evaluating the potential benefits for society of research using genetic technologies". The sub-point "analysing the social implications and ethical uses ..." is b10's; "evaluating the changes to the Earth's biodiversity due to genetic techniques" is b12 and b13's. This video owns first coverage of the two future-direction sub-points; b13 and b19 return to benefits with evidence. Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "researching" is carried by the evidence ladder (scene 5) and the two cases; "evaluating" by scene 9's three questions and attempt 2 (evaluate a claim; what-markers-reward: "Evaluate ... test the thing named in the question against the evidence and reach a supported judgement"). Attempt 1 uses "explain" (what-markers-reward: "name the relevant feature, then show how it causes the stated outcome") and "identify".

design.visualSystem: One evidence ladder at the left of the frame from scene 5 onward: five coded rungs, bottom to top, "only an idea", "works in the lab", "works in animals", "human trials", "approved and in use", each a slim cream bar with a small grey label; cases sit on rungs as small plate thumbnails. Before scene 5 the frame is a mechanism stage: DNA is b01's `SlimStrand` drawn as a double strand (slim, cream bases, no letter tiles), the guide RNA is B6b's terracotta strand at the same slim scale, and Cas9 is a coded translucent rounded enzyme outline (lilac-grey) that clamps the strand; the cut is two short amber nicks, one per strand. The sickle cell case uses the painted `m6-red-cells-normal-sickle-v1.png`, a coded globin-gene strip with two gene blocks ("adult" and "foetal") and a coded switch protein glyph, and a coded flow (cells out, dish, edit, cells back) with `b3a-petri-dish-v1.png` and the new `m6-infusion-bag-cells-v1.png`; no person or body outline. The gene drive uses `m5x-anopheles-mosquito-v1.png`, the new `m6-mosquito-cage-v1.png`, and clean chromosome diagram panels (two slim homologous chromosome outlines side by side, cream, with the drive allele as an amber band; no painted cell behind them), plus a coded offspring row (eight small mosquito glyphs) and a coded population line. Scene 9 has a three-question board ("need", "feasibility", "fairness"). Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey ladder labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The red cells plate and three grey headline strips open the hook; the slim DNA strand takes the guide RNA and the Cas9 outline for the cut; the red cells plate returns with the haemoglobin switch strip; the 30-circle grid and the three-step cost strip build and dim; the evidence ladder draws rung by rung and the treatment thumbnail climbs it; the mosquito plate and chromosome panel show the drive spreading through offspring rows and the female fertility gene; unknown chips write and dim beside the returning headline; the three-question board draws its columns and the "could ... if" line; the memory lines write large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as chains and chips fill; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
